title: Part 91: General Operating Rules
description: Master VFR/IFR flight rules, weather minimums, equipment requirements, and operating limitations from 14 CFR Part 91

questions.question: What are the VFR weather minimums for Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL?
options: 5 SM visibility, 1000' below, 1000' above, 1 SM horizontal
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.155, Class E airspace below 10,000' MSL requires 3 SM visibility and 500' below, 1000' above, 2000' horizontal from clouds.

questions.question: What are the VFR weather minimums for Class B airspace?
options: 5 SM visibility, 1000' below, 1000' above, 1 SM horizontal
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.155, Class B airspace requires 3 SM visibility and clear of clouds.

questions.question: What is the maximum speed below Class B airspace or in a VFR corridor through Class B?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.117, the maximum speed below Class B airspace or in a VFR corridor through Class B is 200 knots indicated.

questions.question: Below 10,000 feet MSL, what is the maximum indicated airspeed?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.117, no person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed greater than 250 knots.

questions.question: Within 4 NM of a Class C or D airport at or below 2,500 feet AGL, the maximum speed is:
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.117, within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or D airspace area at or below 2,500 feet AGL, maximum speed is 200 knots.

questions.question: At what altitude must a pilot use supplemental oxygen?
options: Above 12,500 feet cabin altitude for more than 30 minutes
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.211, above 12,500' through 14,000' cabin altitude, crew must use supplemental oxygen after 30 minutes; above 14,000' at all times.

questions.question: Passengers must be provided supplemental oxygen when the cabin altitude exceeds:
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.211, each occupant must be provided supplemental oxygen when cabin altitude exceeds 15,000 feet.

questions.question: What equipment is required for VFR day flight?
questions.explanation: VFR day requires TOMATO FLAMES: Tachometer, Oil pressure/temp, Manifold pressure (if applicable), Altimeter, Temperature gauge (liquid cooled), Oil quantity, Magnetic compass, Airspeed, Fuel gauges, Landing gear indicator, Anti-collision lights, Manifold pressure (constant-speed prop), ELT, Seatbelts.

questions.question: What additional equipment is required for VFR night flight beyond VFR day?
options: Position lights, anti-collision lights, landing light (for hire), fuses, source of electrical power
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.205(c), VFR night additionally requires FLAPS: Fuses, Landing light (if for hire), Anti-collision lights, Position lights, Source of electrical power.

questions.question: What is the minimum safe altitude over a congested area?
options: 1000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2000-foot radius
1000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2000 feet
500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.119, over congested areas: 1000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2000 feet.

questions.question: What is the minimum safe altitude over other than congested areas?
options: 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.119, over other than congested areas: 500 feet above the surface except within 500 feet of any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.

questions.question: What is the right-of-way rule when two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude?
options: The faster aircraft has the right-of-way
The aircraft on the left shall give way
The aircraft on the right has the right-of-way
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.113, when aircraft of the same category converge at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft on the right has the right-of-way.

questions.question: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over all other air traffic?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.113, an aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic.

questions.question: What is the right-of-way hierarchy among different aircraft categories?
options: Balloon > Glider > Airship > Airplane towing > Powered
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.113: Balloon > Glider > Airship > Airplane/rotorcraft towing > Airplane/rotorcraft.

questions.question: When two aircraft are approaching head-on, each pilot shall:
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.113(e), when aircraft approach head-on or nearly so, each pilot shall alter course to the right.

questions.question: What is the transponder code for VFR flight?
questions.explanation: The standard VFR transponder code is 1200. Emergency codes: 7500 (hijack), 7600 (comm failure), 7700 (emergency).

questions.question: Where is a Mode C transponder required?
options: In and above Class B and C airspace, within 30 NM of Class B primary airport
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.215, Mode C is required in Class A, B, C; within 30 NM of Class B primary airport from surface to 10,000' MSL; and above 10,000' MSL (excluding below 2500' AGL).

questions.question: When must an aircraft have an Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT)?
options: Required for most aircraft, with specific exceptions
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.207, ELT is required for most U.S. registered civil aircraft with exceptions for training flights within 50 NM, ferrying for inspection/installation, etc.

questions.question: What VFR cruising altitude should be used when flying a magnetic course of 180° at 5,500 feet MSL?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.159, VFR cruising altitudes above 3,000' AGL: Magnetic courses 0-179° use odd thousands + 500 (3500, 5500, etc.); 180-359° use even thousands + 500 (4500, 6500, etc.). 180° would use even + 500.

questions.question: What is the fuel reserve requirement for VFR day flight?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.151, VFR day requires enough fuel to fly to first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes reserve at normal cruise speed.

questions.question: What is the fuel reserve requirement for VFR night flight?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.151, VFR night requires enough fuel to fly to first point of intended landing plus 45 minutes reserve at normal cruise speed.

questions.question: What is the fuel reserve requirement for IFR flight?
options: 45 minutes reserve at normal cruise speed
Fly to destination, then alternate, plus 45 minutes at normal cruise
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.167, IFR requires enough fuel to complete flight to destination, fly to alternate (if required), plus 45 minutes at normal cruise speed.

questions.question: When is an alternate airport required for an IFR flight plan?
options: When weather at destination is forecast below VFR minimums
When destination weather is forecast below 2000' ceiling or 3 SM visibility (1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA)
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.169, an alternate is required if destination weather (1 hr before to 1 hr after ETA) is forecast below 2000' ceiling or 3 SM visibility. Remember: '1-2-3 rule'.

questions.question: What is the preflight action required for all flights?
options: Become familiar with all available information concerning the flight
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.103, pilots must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including weather, fuel requirements, runway lengths, and alternatives.

questions.question: For flights not in the vicinity of an airport, preflight action must include:
options: Weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if planned flight cannot be completed
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.103, for flights not in the vicinity of an airport, information must include weather reports/forecasts, fuel requirements, and alternatives.

questions.question: When is ADS-B Out equipment required?
options: In the same airspace that requires a transponder
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.225, ADS-B Out is required in essentially the same airspace as Mode C transponder: Class A, B, C; within 30 NM of Class B; above 10,000' MSL; etc.

questions.question: What must a pilot do before entering Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.131, no person may operate an aircraft in Class B airspace unless ATC has authorized that specific operation.

questions.question: What is required to operate in Class C airspace?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.130, two-way radio communications must be established before entering Class C airspace. Established means ATC has acknowledged aircraft callsign.

questions.question: What constitutes 'established communication' with ATC for Class C/D entry?
questions.explanation: Two-way communication is established when ATC acknowledges your callsign. 'Aircraft calling, standby' is NOT establishment.

questions.question: What is the duration of a Special VFR clearance at night?
options: Special VFR is not permitted at night
Pilot must be instrument rated and aircraft IFR-equipped
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.157, Special VFR at night requires pilot to be instrument rated and aircraft to be IFR-equipped.

questions.question: What are Special VFR weather minimums?
options: Flight visibility 1 SM, remain clear of clouds
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.157, Special VFR requires 1 SM flight visibility and clear of clouds. Ground visibility not applicable.

questions.question: When must position lights be on?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.209, aircraft must display lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise.

questions.question: What is the maximum altitude for VFR flight in Class G airspace at night?
questions.explanation: There is no specific altitude limit for VFR in Class G at night, but weather minimums apply and Class G typically ends at 14,500' MSL.

questions.question: Above 10,000 feet MSL, what are the VFR visibility and cloud clearance requirements?
options: 5 SM visibility, 1000' below, 1000' above, 1 SM horizontal
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.155, above 10,000' MSL: 5 SM visibility, 1000' below, 1000' above, 1 SM horizontal from clouds.

questions.question: What is the minimum visibility for VFR flight in Class G airspace at night below 1,200 feet AGL?
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.155, Class G at night below 1200' AGL requires 3 SM visibility and 500' below, 1000' above, 2000' horizontal.

questions.question: When must seat belts be worn during flight?
options: During takeoff, landing, and when PIC directs
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.107, each person must have their seat belt fastened during takeoff, landing, and at any time the PIC directs.

questions.question: AVFR pilot encounters IMC. What is the appropriate action?
options: Declare emergency and request IFR clearance
Either turn around or, if necessary, request assistance and maintain aircraft control
questions.explanation: VFR into IMC is dangerous. Best action is 180° turn if possible; if not, maintain aircraft control, request assistance, and declare emergency if needed.

questions.question: What is the minimum equipment list (MEL) and when can it be used?
options: An FAA-approved document allowing operations with certain equipment inoperative
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.213, an MEL is an FAA-approved document that allows operations with specific equipment inoperative, as alternative to 91.213(d) Procedures.

questions.question: Without an MEL, what must a pilot do if equipment is inoperative?
options: Determine if equipment is required; if not, placard inoperative and deactivate or remove
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.213(d), without an MEL: determine if equipment is required by regs/AD/equipment list; if not required, placard inoperative, deactivate or remove.

questions.question: What is the pilot's responsibility regarding weather?
options: ATC is responsible for weather avoidance
The pilot is responsible for weather avoidance at all times
Only responsible when radar is inoperative
questions.explanation: The pilot in command is ALWAYS responsible for weather avoidance and safe operation of the aircraft, regardless of ATC radar assistance or flight rules.
